Characterization and genomic analysis of a novel keratinolytic Streptomyces sp. 3–6 for efficient bioconversion of feather waste
works.abstract: The annual accumulation of vast quantities of poultry feather waste poses a significant global challenge to environmental sustainability and resource management. Feathers are protein-rich biomaterials; however, their highly recalcitrant β-keratin structure, stabilized by abundant disulfide bonds, renders them extremely resistant to degradation by conventional biological methods. This inherent recalcitrance contributes to persistent environmental hazards and represents a substantial loss of a potentially valuable biological resource. A novel feather-degrading actinobacterial strain was isolated from soil samples collected at a sea duck farm and identified as Streptomyces sp. 3–6 through integrated morphological, physiological-biochemical and genomic analyses. Optimum fermentation conditions were systematically determined using single factor experiments, Plackett-Burman (PB) screening, and orthogonal optimization, yielding the following parameters: feather, 25.0 g/L; yeast extract, 12.0 g/L; sucrose, 20.0 g/L; MgCl 2 , 4.0 g/L; initial pH, 10.0; and temperature, 30 °C. Under these conditions, strain 3–6 achieved near-complete feather degradation (~90% weight loss) within 120 h, with a maximum keratinase activity of 332.40 ± 11.25 U/mL, 2.64-fold higher than that observed in the basal medium (125.91 U/mL). The crude keratinase exhibited maximal activity at 70 °C and pH 7.0, and demonstrated remarkable pH stability across a broad range (pH 6.0–9.5). Amino acid analysis revealed that the fermentation hydrolysate was enriched in free amino acids, particularly nutritionally essential histidine and leucine. Genome-wide analysis identified sprD , a putative gene predicted to encode a canonical S1-family serine protease, underscoring the strain’s intrinsic genetic capacity for keratinolysis. The novel feather‑degrading actinobacterium Streptomyces sp. 3‑6, isolated from sea duck farm soil and exhibiting robust metabolic adaptability, employs a synergistic enzymatic system comprising keratinase and disulfide reductase to efficiently hydrolyze recalcitrant feather keratin into bioavailable amino acids. This capability positions the strain as a promising biocatalyst for the sustainable valorization of keratinous waste into high-value, protein-rich feed supplements.

works.title: Engineering yeast consortia by partitioning glucose and multiple organic-acid utilization to enhance β-carotene production from simulated distillery wastewater
works.abstract: Synthetic microbial consortia (SMC) have emerged as a promising platform, often outperforming monocultures in metabolic efficiency. Despite this potential, the simultaneous co-utilization of glucose and diverse organic acids in wastewater for value-added chemical production remains a significant technical challenge. In this study, to achieve simultaneous co-utilization of glucose, lactate, and acetate to enable β-carotene production, an engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain Sc -CarLA was first constructed by introducing the lactate utilization pathway from Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and the acetate metabolism pathway from Escherichia coli into the original S. cerevisiae strain Sc -Car. However, severe competition between glucose and organic acids metabolism significantly hindered fermentation, resulting in reduced carbon source consumption and ultimately yielding only 30.9 ± 2.7 mg/L of β-carotene, a ~32% decrease compared to the original strain Sc -Car. To overcome this bottleneck, a novel SMC was first proposed and constructed, which separates the glucose metabolic pathway from the organic acid utilization pathway into two specialized strains. A glucose-specialist strain Sc -CarG1 was constructed by deleting the ADY2 gene, which encodes a vital organic acid transporter, from strain Sc -Car. Concurrently, an organic acids specialist strain, Sc -CarLA2, was constructed by deleting glucose transporter genes GAL2 and HXT1-7 . Subsequently, the co-culture of these two strains, Sc -CarG1 and Sc -CarLA2, exhibited improved fermentation performance, rapidly depleting glucose within 12 h and completely consuming acetate and lactate within 36 h. A two-parallel regulatory strategy, compositional division of labor (DOL) of microbes and temporal DOL, was then employed to further optimize the fermentation performance. As a result, the β-carotene titer in the compositional DOL system reached 64.0 ± 1.5 mg/L at the optimal cell ratio of 1:2 ( Sc -CarG1: Sc -CarLA2). Finally, the temporal DOL system, characterized by the sequential inoculation of the organic acids-specialist strain Sc -CarLA2 followed by the glucose-specific strain Sc -CarG1, enhanced the β-carotene titer to 71.9 ± 2.8 mg/L. A novel SMC that partitions the glucose metabolism pathway and organic acids utilization pathways into two specialist strains was first constructed, efficiently alleviating the bottleneck caused by carbon catabolite repression between glucose and organic acid metabolism, thereby facilitating rapid utilization of carbon sources and significantly boosting β-carotene production.

works.title: Fucoidan and xyloglucan hydrolysis predicted by protein domain architecture in GH29 α-l-fucosidases
works.abstract: Abstract Family GH29 α- l -fucosidases hydrolyze fucosylated glycoconjugates via a retaining mechanism and are therefore considered useful for the synthesis of medically relevant molecules such as α-fucosylated human milk oligosaccharides by transfucosylation using naturally abundant α- l -fucosyl donors. Fucoidan and fucosylated xyloglucan are naturally abundant polysaccharides that can serve as α- l -fucosyl donors. However, few GH29 α- l -fucosidases have been reported to hydrolyze these polysaccharides or use them in transfucosylation, although large-scale efforts have been made to characterize members of this family. Here, we describe a domain-context-based analysis that we employed to predict GH29 α- l -fucosidases likely to hydrolyze fucoidan and fucosylated xyloglucan. We predicted fucoidan- and fucosylated xyloglucan-hydrolyzing α- l -fucosidases based on the presence of co-occurring sulfatase domains, and relevant carbohydrate-binding modules and glycoside hydrolase domains, and fine-tuned our predictions using ecological niche information and Conserved Unique Peptide Patterns grouping. We recombinantly expressed and biochemically characterized seven of these predicted GH29 members from Rhodopirellula sp. SWK7 ( Rs Fuc), Rhodopirellula pilleata ( Rp Fuc), Novipirellula artificiosorum ( Na Fuc), Clostridium methylpentosum ( Cm Fuc), Rhodopirellula maiorica ( Rm Fuc), Bacteroides sp. ( Bs Fuc), and Bacterium HR17/ Candidatus Fervidibacter japonicus (HR17Fuc), and demonstrated that they catalyze the hydrolysis of fucoidan and fucosylated xyloglucan. While these α- l -fucosidases did not score positive in a cursory transfucosylation screen, these and other GH29 members predicted to hydrolyze fucoidan or fucosylated xyloglucan may be further explored for their transfucosylation potential in future studies. The domain-context-based prediction of substrate preference described here can be extended for other substrates and to other carbohydrate-active enzyme families. Key points • GH29 alpha-L-fucosidases with fucoidan or xyloglucan-specific domains were predicted • RsFuc, RpFuc, NaFuc, CmFuc, RmFuc, BsFuc, and HR17Fuc were recombinantly expressed • Fucoidan and fucosylated xyloglucan were hydrolyzed by these alpha-L-fucosidases

works.title: New virus-free insect cell lines derived from BTI-TN-5B1-4 exhibit high performance in recombinant protein production
works.abstract: Abstract The Trichoplusia ni -derived BTI-TN-5B1-4 (Tn5) cell line, commonly referred to as High Five ™ , is widely used for recombinant protein production because of its high productivity and strong secretion capacity in the baculovirus-insect cell expression system. However, adventitious viral contamination remains a significant concern, particularly in the manufacture of vaccines and therapeutic proteins, for which ensuring viral safety is paramount. In 2007, a latent infection with Tn5 Cell Line Virus (TnCLV), a member of the genus Alphanodavirus, was identified in Tn5 cells. Here, we report the discovery of a second adventitious virus, Bombyx mori macula-like virus (BmMLV), in the Tn5 cell line, and demonstrate that both viruses can be successfully eliminated using a co-culture protocol with Sf9 cells across a permeable membrane. Clonal cell lines were established from the resulting virus-free Tn5 cells and comprehensively characterized in serum-free suspension culture. Selected lines exhibited growth kinetics comparable to those of commercial High Five cells, supported productive baculovirus infection, and achieved recombinant protein yields comparable to or higher than those of High Five cells. These products included secreted alkaline phosphatase (SEAP), β-galactosidase (β-gal), the adenovirus penton-based virus-like particle ADDomer, and the malaria vaccine candidate PfRipr5. These new, fully traceable, virus-free cell lines provide an enhanced biosafety profile, potentially increasing their suitability for regulated biomanufacturing, and represent robust and reliable platforms for high-level recombinant protein production in both research and industrial applications.

works.title: Systematic regulation of mycelial extracellular proteolysis, endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis, morphology, and bioprocess boosts recombinant laccase production in Coprinopsis cinerea
works.abstract: Laccase is an important green catalyst, particularly basidiomycete laccases, which have significant industrial applications in fields, such as food and biomass energy. However, the natural secretion of laccase by basidiomycetes is low. Heterologous expression of basidiomycete laccase in yeast or Aspergillus often changes the enzyme's properties due to inappropriate post-translational modifications. Therefore, using basidiomycetes for homologous recombination expression of basidiomycete laccase has great industrial prospects and economic benefits. This study used the native host for the homologous recombination expression of Laccase Lcc5 from Coprinopsis cinerea and developed a novel strategy to increase its extracellular activity. Silencing the protease Ccmpr , overexpressing the endoplasmic reticulum stress response gene Anhac 1, and silencing the morphological regulation gene rac 1 all increased the recombinant Lcc5 activity. The extracellular laccase activity of the rac 1-silenced Cc lcc5 -anti rac 1-2 was 1.84-fold higher than that of the original Cc lcc5 -13. In particular, the Cc lcc5 -anti ChiE 2& mpr -3, obtained by simultaneously silencing the chitinase ChiE2 and the protease Ccmpr , exhibited the highest extracellular laccase activity, 67.71 U/mL, which was 2.56-fold higher than that of Cc lcc5 -13. Optimizing the fermentation process of Cc lcc5 -anti ChiE 2& mpr -3 increased laccase activity in shake flasks to 76.03 U/mL when using 20 g/L yeast extract as the nitrogen source. At a stirring speed of 200 rpm, the laccase activity in a 1.5-L fermenter reached 109.95 U/mL. To our knowledge, this is the highest extracellular laccase Lcc5 activity in basidiomycetes reported to date. This is the first report of a multidimensional integrated strategy to enhance recombinant protein expression in C. cinerea by modulating protease gene expression, optimizing post-translational folding and secretion, and modifying mycelial morphology. This study will pave the way for laccase industrial production and accelerate the development of the C. cinerea high-expression system.

Next‐Generation Electrochemical Analytical Systems: A Critical Review of Biosensing Technologies, Miniaturized Platforms, and Future Intelligent Diagnostics
works.abstract: Electrochemical analytical systems have evolved from conventional sensing devices into advanced platforms capable of real-time monitoring, multiplexed analysis, and decentralized diagnostics. Progress in biosensing technologies, nanomaterials, microfluidics, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence has significantly improved analytical performance and expanded potential applications in healthcare, environmental monitoring, and food safety. This review critically evaluates recent advances in next-generation electrochemical analytical systems, focusing on biosensing technologies, nanomaterial-enabled platforms, miniaturized devices, precision diagnostics, and emerging intelligent analytical systems, and identifies the major barriers to their practical implementation. Advanced electrochemical biosensors, including enzymatic, immunosensors, aptasensors, nucleic acid sensors, and molecularly imprinted polymer-based platforms, have demonstrated remarkable sensitivity and selectivity. Nanomaterials such as graphene, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), MXenes, and metal nanoparticles have further enhanced signal amplification and electron-transfer efficiency. In parallel, miniaturized technologies, including screen-printed electrodes (SPE), paper-based devices, microfluidic systems, and wearable sensors, have accelerated point-of-care diagnostics. However, persistent challenges related to matrix effects, biofouling, reproducibility, standardization, long-term stability, clinical validation, and manufacturing scalability continue to hinder widespread translation. The future of electrochemical analytical systems lies in developing robust, standardized, and clinically validated intelligent diagnostic ecosystems that integrate advanced sensing technologies with artificial intelligence, digital connectivity, and automated data analysis. Achieving successful clinical translation will require greater emphasis on reproducibility, regulatory compliance, multicenter validation, and real-world applicability, rather than solely on achieving ever-lower detection limits.

works.title: Biostimulation Sustains a Carbonic Anhydrase‐Producing Bacterial Consortium for CO 2 Hydration and Residual Oil Utilization Under Simulated Reservoir Conditions
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Depleted oil reservoirs are potential targets for geological CO 2 storage; however, temperature, salinity, pressure, and nutrient scarcity can suppress microbial activity. In this study, a consortium comprising the carbonic‐anhydrase‐producing bacterium Bacillus licheniformis S5 and the petroleum‐degrading bacterium Bacillus cereus S0 was evaluated in a stirred high‐pressure liquid system containing simulated brine and residual crude oil. Nitrogen and phosphorus biostimulation promoted culturable growth. At 50°C and 10 MPa, the S5 + S0 consortium maintained higher colony‐forming unit (CFU) counts and more persistent apparent carbonic‐anhydrase‐associated esterase activity than either monoculture. S0‐mediated crude‐oil degradation produced fatty‐acid intermediates and surface‐active metabolites, reducing surface tension to 62.14 mN/m and increasing aqueous CO 2 mass transfer. Meanwhile, S5‐associated carbonic anhydrase activity promoted CO 2 hydration, and the consortium maintained HCO 3 − concentrations above 900 mg/L. Collectively, these findings support a bench‐scale mechanistic framework in which residual‐oil utilization, interfacial modification, and enzymatically mediated CO 2 hydration are functionally coupled under simulated reservoir‐fluid conditions. This framework provides a foundation for subsequent evaluation in oil‐bearing rock microcosms and core‐flood systems.

works.title: PHA Production and Wastewater Treatment With Phototrophic Purple Bacteria: Effect of Transitioning OLR and HRT on Biopolymer Composition and Process Yield
works.abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigated the effect of transitioning organic loading rates (OLR) and hydraulic retention times (HRT) on polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) production from wastewater using PHA‐accumulating phototrophic purple bacteria. These bacteria were cultivated under light‐feast anaerobic conditions in a photo‐assisted continuous stirred tank reactor (P‐CSTR) fed with acidogenic fermented cattle manure and sugarcane molasses. Transitioning OLRs of 0.7, 1.6, and 2.0 g COD/L.d were tested, followed by HRTs of 48, 72, and 112 h at the optimal OLR. The desired conditions to boost PHA production were an OLR of 0.7–1.2 g COD/L.d and HRT of 112 h, attaining a maximum PHA accumulation of 86.3% g PHA/g VSS, and production yield of 94.5% g COD PHA /g COD removed . The system also indicated efficient pollutant elimination of 96.6% NH 4 ‐N, and 82.5% COD. Shorter HRTs (48 h) were less effective in COD removal but promoted higher poly‐3‐hydroxyvalerate production in the copolymer content (48.8% of PHA). In contrast, poly‐3‐hydroxybutyrate content increased at high OLRs. The results highlight that transitioning OLR and varying HRT significantly influenced the process performance, PHA accumulation yield, and biopolymer quality. Thus, OLR and HRT are the critical control parameters for optimizing PHA production, tailoring polymer properties, and ensuring enhanced wastewater treatment.

works.title: A bioluminescence immunosensor using engineered antibody for quantitative detection of African swine fever virus
works.abstract: Abstract African swine fever (ASF), caused by ASF virus (ASFV), poses a significant threat to global swine industries due to its high mortality and the lack of an effective vaccine. Consequently, it is critical to develop a rapid and quantitative detection method for timely monitoring of swine populations and accurate confirmation of ASF infection, thereby enhancing ASF prevention and control measures. Here, we developed an ultrasensitive bioluminescence immunosensor for quantitative detection of ASFV p30 (p30-UBI) by genetically fusing HiBiT (an 11-amino-acid peptide that binds the NanoLuc fragment LgBiT with high affinity, reconstituting bright bioluminescence) to the light chain constant region of monoclonal antibody (mAb) 16-5E7E8 as the detection antibody and using mAb 2-1B3G3 as the capture antibody. The p30-UBI exhibited broad linear ranges of 46 pg/mL to 250 ng/mL for recombinant p30 protein (a combined quantitative range covered by two calibration equations) with detection limits of 15.3 pg/mL. The practical utility of the p30-UBI was evaluated using tissue, serum, and swab samples from ASFV-challenged pigs. P30 was readily detectable in tissue and serum samples, whereas lower concentrations were measured in swabs, and p30 levels showed broadly similar patterns to ASFV p72 gene copy numbers determined by quantitative PCR (qPCR). Notably, in an exploratory analysis in which pigs from different vaccine groups and dose groups were combined, lower serum p30 levels at 7 dpc were significantly associated with longer survival after ASFV challenge (Spearman ρ = − 0.62, P < 0.0001, n = 53). These findings indicate that the p30-UBI is a promising quantitative analytical method evaluated in samples from experimentally infected pigs. Key points • A HiBiT-tagged antibody-based bioluminescence immunosensor was developed for ASFV p30 detection • The assay achieves detection limits of 15.3 pg/mL for p30 within 70 min • Lower serum p30 levels at 7 dpc were associated with longer survival in an exploratory analysis

Bacillus subtilis as a heterologous host for production and secretion of a hyperthermostable archaeal subtilisin-like protease
works.abstract: Abstract Pernisine is a subtilisin-like protease from the hyperthermophilic archaeon Aeropyrum pernix . Its ability to degrade resistant protein substrates such as prion proteins makes this protease attractive for industrial applications. Here, we used Bacillus subtilis as a heterologous host for expression and secretion prepropernisine, a precursor of pernisine. The native secretion signal peptide of prepropernisine was replaced with a signal peptide of native B. subtilis preprosubtilisin E to achieve efficient secretion. Among the four promoters tested, xylose-inducible promoter yielded the highest level of propernisine production, with a titer of 175 mg per l of culture. The produced propernisine was purified from the culture medium using a combination of ultrafiltration, anion-exchange chromatography, and heat treatment. Approximately 115 mg of propernisine with 80% purity was obtained per liter of culture, representing a 10-fold higher yield than previously achieved with other heterologous hosts. Activated pernisine obtained from B. subtilis exhibited remarkably high thermostability, with optimal activity at temperatures above 90 °C and across a pH range of 7 to 9. In addition, it retained approximately 60% of initial activity after autoclaving and efficiently degraded collagen and meat. The stability and performance of pernisine from B. subtilis were nearly identical to that of pernisine produced in Escherichia coli . Overall, these findings demonstrate that B. subtilis is a promising host for further optimization of cultivation conditions and scale-up to controlled bioreactor cultivation, to achieve production of pernisine at industrial level. Key points • Bacillus subtilis efficiently produced and secreted recombinant propernisine. • Propernisine was readily purified from the culture medium. • Activated pernisine exhibited high thermostability and efficient meat hydrolysis.

L-Threonine production from acetate by metabolically engineered Corynebacterium glutamicum using a pH-controlled fed-batch process
works.abstract: Acetate has a considerable potential as a non-food feedstock for microbial bioproduction, yet its use for amino acid production remains underexplored. Here, we developed a process for L-threonine production from acetate as the sole carbon source with Corynebacterium glutamicum by integrating rational, genome-based metabolic engineering with pH-coupled fed-batch cultivation. The engineered strain AT-3 carried five chromosomal mutations that alleviated feedback inhibition of key enzymes and redirected carbon flux toward the aspartate pathway. Substrate supply was controlled using a custom Visual Basic-based feeding script that automatically adjusted the acetic acid feed in response to online pH measurements. Robust process performance was maintained during a tenfold scale-up from 100-mL DASbox to 1-L DASGIP bioreactors. The optimized process achieved an L-threonine titer of 10.04 g/L and a yield of 0.086 g/g acetate. This study provides a basis for further studies on the development and improvement of acetate-based amino acid production process. KEY POINTS: • Plasmid-free C. glutamicum strains produce L-threonine in acetate minimal medium • pH-controlled acetic acid feed in bioreactors improved L-threonine production • Acetate-based production of feed amino acids avoids competition with human food.

works.title: Characterization of the lysine-forming saccharopine dehydrogenase Lys1 from filamentous fungi
works.abstract: Abstract Lysine biosynthesis in fungi proceeds through the α-aminoadipate pathway with Lys1 (EC 1.5.1.7) catalyzing the final reversible L-lysine producing step. Although Lys1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been characterized, limited information is available on this highly conserved enzyme in filamentous fungi relevant for solid-state food fermentation. Here, we compare Lys1 homologs from Aspergillus nidulans, Penicillium roqueforti, and Rhizopus microsporus with the S. cerevisiae enzyme as reference using phylogenetic, biophysical, kinetic, and molecular dynamics analyses. Sequence and structural comparisons showed sequence divergence across fungal lineages while overall fold and key catalytic residues were conserved. All enzymes displayed strong directional pH dependence, with the forward L-lysine producing reaction favored at alkaline pH and the reverse reaction promoted at neutral pH. Analyses of temperature profile revealed homolog-specific differences, with the homolog from S. cerevisiae presenting the highest temperature optimum and melting temperature. The turnover (kcat) of the reverse reaction was consistently higher than the forward reaction for all homologs, consistent with thermodynamic constraints on lysine formation. Kinetic characterization revealed that the S. cerevisiae enzyme had the highest kcat, followed by A. nidulans and P. roqueforti, whereas the R. microsporus enzyme had lower activity and highest activation energy. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborated that the more active homologs more frequently sampled near-reactive NAD⁺ C4-saccharopine C8 geometries, while R. microsporus showed lower sampling frequency of these conformations and weaker protein–ligand contact organization. These findings provide a mechanistic and kinetic basis for understanding lysine biosynthesis in filamentous fungi. Key points • Phylogenetic, biophysical, kinetic, molecular dynamics of Lys1 from fungi • Catalytic residues and Lys1 folds are conserved (LDDT > 0.9) but sequences differ • Reaction direction (saccharopine ↔ L-lysine) is strongly dependent on pH

works.title: Understanding the molecular-level responses of cattle rumen microbiota to kaolin clay as a feed additive in vitro
works.abstract: Abstract Enteric methane emissions from ruminants, primarily produced by methanogenic archaea during rumen fermentation, contribute substantially to greenhouse gas emissions and represent a loss of dietary energy. Clay mineral-based feed additives have been explored as potential methane mitigation strategies; however, their mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study investigated the mechanistic role of halloysite–kaolinite mixed mineral (kaolin) supplementation in modulating rumen fermentation and microbial functional potential, including bacteria, protozoa, and archaea, using an in vitro system. Approximately 5% clay was incorporated into 2 g of basal diet and incubated under anaerobic conditions using ANKOM technology. Samples were collected at defined intervals up to 48 h, and integrated 16S and 18S rRNA sequencing, and PICRUSt2 functional prediction analyses. Clay supplementation reduced methane by ~21%, from 35.43 ± 3.50 to 27.85 ± 2.31 mL CH 4 /g dry matter. Although bacterial and archaeal community composition shifted in response to supplementation, the dominant bacterial taxa ( Firmicutes and Bacteroidota ), and protozoal populations were largely preserved. Predicted methanogenesis pathway abundance was significantly reduced by ~47% ( p < 0.01), alongside methane reduction. Predicted functional analysis further revealed potential alteration in enzyme-mediated hydrogen utilisation ( p < 0.001). This might indicate a redistribution of metabolic hydrogen among competing pathways without accumulation. Microscopic observations further showed spatial associations between microbial cells and clay surfaces. These findings suggest that kaolin reduces methane production through changes in predicted functional potential related to methanogenesis and hydrogen utilisation, alongside shifts in bacterial and archaeal community composition, while fermentation-related parameters remained largely stable. Key points • Kaolin clay in feed suppresses rumen methanogenesis without disrupting fermentation or fibre digestion. • Clay may redirect hydrogen away from methane production, offering a practical methane-mitigation strategy. • Direct microbial attachment to clay coincided with altered predicted methanogenesis potential, while dominant taxa were largely preserved.

works.title: Rhizopus stolonifer as a biocatalyst for cyclic dipeptide production and artemisinin/artemether biotransformation
works.abstract: Abstract Fungi are prolific producers of chemically diverse natural products and biocatalytically active enzymes, yet the biosynthetic and biotransformation potential of many fungal species remains underexplored. This study establishes Rhizopus stolonifer as a promising platform for both natural-product discovery and selective biotransformation of bioactive molecules. Ten cyclic dipeptides (CDPs) and over seventy additional metabolites were tentatively identified using an integrated metabolomics approach combining gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and one- and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Three major CDPs, cyclo(L-Leu-L-Pro), cyclo(L-Ile-L-Pro), and cyclo(L-Phe-L-Pro), were subsequently isolated and characterized, with their stereochemical configurations established. In parallel, R. stolonifer was utilized as a microbial platform for the biotransformation of antimalarial drugs artemisinin and artemether. The resulting derivatives were generated through deoxygenation, site-selective hydroxylation, and structural rearrangement. Time-course NMR analyses provided evidence for the proposed biotransformation pathways. Genome mining revealed six putative non-ribosomal peptide synthetase biosynthetic gene clusters and thirteen cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, suggesting a genetic basis for CDP biosynthesis and artemisinin biotransformation, respectively. These results underscore the dual utility of R. stolonifer as a rich source of CDPs and a versatile biocatalyst for the transformation of artemisinin derivatives. Key points Rhizopus stolonifer is a rich source of cyclic dipeptides (CDPs). R. stolonifer biotransforms artemisinin and artemether into multiple derivatives. Non-ribosomal peptide synthetase pathways may underpin CDP production.

works.title: Prospective role of proteolytic microorganisms from fermented foods in degradation of gluten and their implications for celiac disease
works.abstract: Abstract Gluten, the main storage protein in wheat, barley, and rye, contains sequences rich in proline and glutamine that resist complete gastrointestinal degradation resulting in generation of immunogenic peptides. The peptides contain immunogenic epitopes that, following deamidation by tissue transglutaminase 2 (TG2), can be presented by HLA-DQ2/DQ8 molecules to gluten-specific CD4 + T cells, resulting in intestinal inflammation. This gluten-induced intestinal inflammation is known as celiac disease (CD) in susceptible individuals. A gluten-free diet (GFD) has been recognised as gold standard treatment to date, which requires lifelong strict compliance, therefore demanding alternative novel therapies. Fermented foods have emerged as promising reservoirs for selection of gluten-degrading probiotic strains as adjunctive therapeutic candidates. These strains may hydrolyse gluten and its immunogenic gluten peptides through specialised array of proteolytic enzymatic systems comprising endopeptidases, prolyl endopeptidases, aminopeptidases and dipeptidyl peptidases. This review critically examines the significance of gluten-degrading microorganisms with probiotic potential from fermented foods and their proteolytic enzyme system. Owing to their origin from fermented foods, the effect of fermentation parameters such as pH, strain selection, and substrate composition is also highlighted. The assessment of studies indicates that the fermentation mediated by selected gluten-degrading strains reduces the gluten content; however, these did not detoxify the immunogenic peptides completely. The potential strains support intestinal health through modulation of gut microbiota and attenuation of inflammatory responses which has been validated through in vitro and clinical studies, although their efficacy in managing CD remains unestablished. However, strain-specific differences, incomplete degradation of immunogenic peptides, and the lack of standardised protocols for evaluating gluten detoxification remain significant barriers to their application. Key points Fermented foods serve as a key reservoir for gluten-degrading microorganismsStrain-specific enzymes and fermentation conditions affect gluten hydrolysis.Clinical efficacy of potential strains has yet to be conclusively established.

Continuous Capture of Recombinant Adeno‐Associated Virus Particles Using Twin‐Column CaptureSMB
works.abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated viruses (rAAVs) have gained increasing importance in gene therapy due to their safe and precise gene delivery. However, certain indications require substantially higher vector doses, pushing manufacturing capacity and cost of goods (COG) to its limits. In this study, we present a proof-of-concept evaluation of a continuous twin-column capture process (CaptureSMB) enabling direct purification of rAAV5 from minimally processed, nonlysed perfusion harvest without prior enzymatic nuclease digestion, concentration or buffer exchange. This approach differs fundamentally from conventional batch workflows which typically mandate clarification and concentration before affinity capture and offers a novel process integration in viral vector manufacturing. A single-column batch capture process was developed first and subsequently compared to continuous CaptureSMB configurations. Optimized CaptureSMB operation achieved consistent yields over four cycles, with recoveries exceeding batch operation (+14.3%) with concomitant higher productivity (+11.4%) and reduced buffer consumption (-79.2%). Critical quality attribute (CQA) analysis showed lower host cell protein levels and lower residual DNA in early CaptureSMB cycles, while full capsid ratios, thermal stability and transduction efficiency of rAAV5 particles remained unaltered across cycles and process modes. However, progressive backpressure and residual impurity accumulation in later cycles highlight operational challenges associated with direct capture of low-titer feed streams. These findings highlight that continuous twin-column CaptureSMB directly from secretion-derived perfusion harvest can improve operational efficiency, lower buffer requirements, and also maintain and, in some respects, enhance product quality. This novel strategy provides a promising route to address manufacturing capacity and cost challenges in rAAV gene therapy production.

works.title: Enabling Raman Spectroscopy‐Based Cell Culture Process Control via Real‐Time Chemometric Model Calibration
works.abstract: Raman spectroscopy, combined with chemometric models such as Partial Least Squares (PLS), is a powerful enabling technology for real-time monitoring and control of industrial cell culture processes. Specifically, the non-destructiveness and near-real time measurement nature of the technology offers great potential in how processes are designed, monitored, and controlled, yet its implementation in industrial settings has been limited. This is mainly due to extensive dataset requirements for chemometric model development, as dozens to hundreds of cell‑culture constituents are known to contribute to Raman scattering effects. Experimental artifacts and anomalies arising from different sites, scales, or equipment further exacerbate this issue. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel one‑point calibration methodology that reframes the model training and validation paradigm from the "best chemometric model for the historical data" to the "best model for the most recent and representative data". Implemented within an adaptive‑learning framework, this approach drastically reduces dependence on extensive historical datasets while better accommodating site-, process-, and run-to-run- variabilities for the 9-14 day fed‑batch Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cell culture processes investigated.

works.title: A Microfluidic TFF Device for Biopharmaceutical Process Development: Scale‐Down Verification of Ultrafiltration and Diafiltration Modes for Monoclonal Antibodies
works.abstract: Tangential flow filtration (TFF) is an essential operation in downstream bioprocessing, yet conventional scale-down models require large material volumes and often fail to capture scale-relevant hydrodynamics. A microfluidic TFF (µTFF) platform was developed that preserves wall shear rate and transmembrane pressure, enabling low-volume investigation of UF/DF processes. Through iterative design of channel geometry and membrane selection, the final device achieved stable operation, high recovery, and a reduced runtime of 2.33 h from feed volumes as low as 10 mL for UF and 1 mL for DF. When operated at matched shear, the µTFF platform captured key bench-scale filtration characteristics, including filtration time, TMP behavior, permeate-flux profiles, and yields above 88% with negligible permeate loss. The device also resolved membrane-dependent behavior across PES and RC chemistries, showing consistent cross-scale trends for PES membranes while highlighting the influence of membrane-specific variability on RC membrane performance and cross-scale comparability. Validated with BSA and subsequently with monoclonal antibodies, the µTFF system demonstrated reproducible buffer exchange, maintained protein integrity, and replicated key transport phenomena. Its low working volumes, rapid turnaround, and ability to maintain scale-relevant hydrodynamics position the µTFF platform as a high-throughput screening tool for TFF process optimization, supporting faster development cycles and evaluation of purification strategies.

works.title: Engineered Magneto‐Receptive E. coli
works.abstract: Naturally occurring magnetotactic bacteria have an inherent ability to sense and align to earth's geomagnetic field due to the presence of magnetosomes-membranous microstructures containing iron oxide nanoparticles. These functionalities can be exploited for tuning movements and guided spatial patterning in controlled magnetic field. While being arduous to culture in laboratories, these organisms have complex genetic make-up with tight regulation on their magnetosome synthesis. Inspired by the magnetotactic bacteria, we aim to render magnetic behavior to E. coli. We mimic the magnetosomes in magnetotactic bacteria by employing a membraneless proteinaceous compartment from the thermophilic iron storage protein, ferritin, fused with a magnetite-forming peptide, m6A. To enhance iron accumulation, the E. coli iron metabolism is engineered by tailoring the expression of iron influx and efflux genes. Numerical simulations support our observations of a highly responsive magnetic E. coli. This study presents a strategy to engineer magnetic response in E. coli which can be adopted to other bacteria.

works.title: L-Lysine production from glucose and chitin monomers using engineered Vibrio natriegens
works.abstract: Abstract Despite its industrial importance, microbial L-lysine production has largely been confined to classical producer strains, leaving the fast-growing, non-pathogenic marine bacterium V. natriegens mostly unexplored as an emerging biosynthetic platform. In this work, we established an L-lysine-overproducing V. natriegens DSM759 strain through a stepwise rational engineering strategy targeting the native biosynthetic pathway. Building on our prior systems-level analysis of the strain’s genetic and regulatory architecture, we identified key metabolic bottlenecks and targeted interventions to relieve them. The central intervention was relief of feedback inhibition on the two key regulatory enzymes, aspartate kinase (AK, lysC ) and dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS, dapA ). Transferring feedback resistance substitutions previously characterized in E. coli to conserved positions in the V. natriegens DSM759 enzymes produced L-lysine-insensitive variants with kinetic parameters comparable to the corresponding wild-type enzymes. Among the tested configurations, the strain co-expressing Vn.lysC2 and Vn.dapA1 :E84T reached the highest L-lysine titer (9.0 ± 0.6 mM) and yield (0.11 ± 0.01 mol Lys mol Glc −1 ), whereas overexpression of additional L-lysine pathway genes provided no further benefit. Exploiting the host’s substrate range, we further demonstrated L-lysine synthesis from the chitin-derived amino sugar N-acetylglucosamine (0.09 ± 0.00 mol Lys mol GlcNAc −1 ), highlighting the potential to valorize chitin-rich waste streams from the seafood industry. This work establishes a minimal rational strategy for L-lysine biosynthesis in V. natriegens DSM759 and positions it as a candidate platform for sustainable amino acid production. Key points • E. coli-derived rational engineering strategies were transferable to V. natriegens • Native pathway deregulation was sufficient to enable L-lysine production • Chitin-derived N-acetylglucosamine supports L-lysine synthesis

works.title: Comprehensive analysis of zearalenone exposure and molecular effects in Rhodococcus pyridinivorans K404
works.abstract: Abstract Zearalenone (ZEA) is a Fusarium-derived mycotoxin that contaminates cereal crops and persists in soils and aquatic environments. Microbial biodegradation is increasingly proposed as a sustainable remediation strategy; however, a critical but often overlooked question is whether chemical disappearance of a toxin reflects actual detoxification. Here, we investigated the biotransformation of ZEA by Rhodococcus pyridinivorans K404 using an integrated analytical, toxicological, and molecular framework using time-resolved chemical profiling, bioluminescent yeast estrogen screening (BLYES/BLYR), zebrafish embryo toxicity assays, and transcriptome-wide RNA-sequencing. Although strain K404 reduced the ZEA concentration in the culture supernatant by up to 90.3% within 72 h, substantial amounts of ZEA and its metabolites were associated with the bacterial pellet, indicating that extracellular depletion reflected both biotransformation and redistribution into a cell-associated fraction. This decrease in supernatant ZEA concentration did not translate into a proportional decrease in biological hazard. In microinjection experiments, treated samples showed significantly higher developmental toxicity; embryo mortality peaked at 72% after 48-h treatments before falling to 53% at 120 h. This transient increase in toxicity aligned with accumulation of hydroxylated metabolites, mainly β-zearalenol and α-zearalenol, implicating biotransformation intermediates as key causes of acute toxicity. The bacterial strain showed a stress-associated transcriptional profile, dominated by genes of iron acquisition and oxidative stress defense. These results demonstrate that microbial ZEA degradation can transiently heighten toxicological risk, instead of reducing it, underscoring that microbial biocontrol strategies in agroecosystems must not rely solely on chemical depletion data but require comprehensive toxicological assessment, particularly through chronic exposure and long-term ecotoxicity studies. Key points • Rhodococcus pyridinivorans K404 efficiently removed ZEA (up to 90.3% in 72 h) • Transient toxicity increased via metabolites, while ZEA estrogenicity declined. • Transcriptomics at 48 h links peak cellular stress to metabolite driven toxicity.

works.title: Comparison of enzymes and amyloid hexapeptide for antibiofilm activity
works.abstract: Abstract This study screened and evaluated a panel of enzymes for their capacities to inhibit biofilm formation and disperse established biofilms, and compared their efficiencies with our previously developed amyloid hexapeptide GI6. Seven enzymes (mutanase, dextranase, collagenase I, dispase II, cellulase, lysozyme, and Dispersin B) and GI6 were evaluated against Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) for anti-biofilm, bactericidal, and biofilm eradication activities. A human enamel block caries model was established, and the anti-biofilm and anti-caries effects were characterized by TEM, CLSM, SEM, and micro-CT. Among the seven enzymes under the tested conditions, only DspB (0.25 mg/mL) showed anti-biofilm activity. Immunofluorescence staining confirmed the presence of the DspB substrate poly‑N‑acetylglucosamine (PNAG) in S. mutans biofilms. Like GI6, DspB lacked bactericidal activity and could not disperse established biofilms. SEM and TEM confirmed reduced extracellular polysaccharides (EPS) and non-bactericidal effects for both. In the human enamel block caries model, both DspB and GI6 inhibited biofilm formation and reduced enamel demineralization, with GI6 showing better efficacy at a lower concentration. These findings indicate that most tested enzymes are ineffective against S. mutans biofilm under the tested conditions, and that DspB inhibits biofilm formation only at higher concentrations than GI6, suggesting that GI6 exhibits superior antibiofilm efficacy and anti-caries activity under the tested conditions. Future efforts in caries prevention may benefit from more effective biofilm-disrupting agents. Key points • Both DspB and GI6 decrease biofilm formation, but fail to disrupt mature biofilms. • GI6 suppresses biofilm formation and enamel demineralization at lower concentrations than DspB. • Agents that more efficiently targeting EPS in mature biofilms would have caries superior prevention value.

works.title: Pilot- to field-scale evaluation of a two-stage vertical flow constructed wetland system for piggery wastewater treatment
works.abstract: Abstract Piggery wastewater is a high-strength effluent requiring efficient and sustainable treatment solutions. This study evaluates a two-stage vertical flow constructed wetland (VFCW) system through pilot- to field-scale investigation, with emphasis on hydraulic loading, passive aeration, and techno-economic feasibility. At pilot scale, the system was operated at flow rates of 4–6 L day⁻1. At 4 L day⁻1 (OLR: 653.4 ± 43 g m⁻2 day⁻1), optimal performance was achieved. The control wetland (CW) exhibited removal efficiencies of 88.95 ± 3.12% (COD), 86.32 ± 5.48% (TOC), 87.71 ± 1.12% (phosphate), 73.37 ± 4.95% (TAN), and 51.25 ± 3.46% (TN). In comparison, the passively aerated system (CW-A) showed improved performance, achieving 90.36 ± 2.98% (COD), 89.68 ± 3.87% (TOC), 90.23 ± 0.98% (phosphate), 87.23 ± 4.23% (TAN), and 67.12 ± 4.23% (TN). Passive aeration achieved using perforated pipes inserted within the VFCW, significantly enhanced nitrogen removal, particularly through improved ammonium oxidation and overall nitrogen transformation, while having only marginal effects on organic matter and phosphate removal. Based on pilot-scale results, scale-up was performed by maintaining a comparable organic loading rate, and a field-scale system treating 7200 L day⁻1 (OLR: 604.3 ± 90.6 g m⁻2 day⁻1) was implemented. The system achieved overall removals of 87.85 ± 12.47% (COD), 86.35 ± 12.08% (TOC), 91.08 ± 10.63% (phosphate), 81.02 ± 13.13% (TAN), 60.45 ± 12.74% (nitrate), and 64.86 ± 13.62% (TN). Stable performance was achieved after a 4–5 week stabilization period, with resilience to influent variability. Techno-economic analysis indicated a treatment cost of ₹45.5 ($ 0.48) m⁻3 and low energy consumption (0.16 kWh m⁻3). The results demonstrate that OLR-based scale-up enables reliable field performance, confirming VFCWs as a robust and cost-effective solution for decentralized piggery wastewater treatment. Key points • OLR-based scale-up ensured successful pilot to field translation. • Passive aeration enhanced TAN and TN removal whereas field-scale system achieved > 85% COD and TOC removal in VFCW. • Low-cost (₹45.5/m3) and energy-efficient (0.16 kWh/m3) treatment. Toward industrial microalgae-based monoclonal antibody production
works.abstract: Over the past two decades, Chinese hamster ovary cells have dominated monoclonal antibody (mAb) production. Although this mammalian cell system carries high operational and capital costs, it aligns well with regulatory requirements for producing high-value, modest-scale therapeutics. However, microalgal systems offer the benefits of light-driven growth, low-cost media, and the potential for significant and efficient scalability, providing a promising route for producing lower-cost mAbs. Reducted production costs and increased scale open novel market opportunities well beyond the therapeutic space. Here, we investigate the history of mAb production in microalgae, the recent molecular and bioprocessing advances that are likely to contribute to their industrial production, and the novel applications that could arise given access to lower-cost mAbs.

Editing dual-function susceptibility genes for multistress-resilient crops
works.abstract: Climate change increasingly exposes crops to simultaneous abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity, and heat, alongside disease, yet crop improvement often treats these threats as separate objectives. We argue that suitable susceptibility (S) genes should be considered as potential dual-function targets in crop biotechnology and breeding. Inactivating S genes can improve disease resistance and abiotic stress tolerance; we term genes with experimental support for both benefits as dual-function S genes. We propose to prioritise these genes and their orthologs in many crops and to screen candidates in both directions by testing S genes for abiotic stress benefits and testing negative abiotic stress regulators for disease resistance. With CRISPR technologies and regulatory frameworks maturing, such editing could support the development of climate-ready crops.

works.title: Biotechnology has outgrown the organism
works.abstract: Synthetic biology increasingly produces hybrid constructs that blur the boundaries of organism-based biosafety regulation. We propose using the term 'biological entity', defined by its capacity to interact meaningfully with biological systems or to facilitate biological processes, as an initial screening category before regulatory classification, enabling more coherent and proportionate oversight.

works.title: A practical guide to vascularized microphysiological systems
works.abstract: Microphysiological systems (MPS) are emerging as human-relevant models for pharmaceutical research, reducing reliance on animal testing. Despite progress in reproducing organ-specific features, integrating functional microvasculature remains challenging. Advances have expanded the number of available options, making it difficult to identify the most suitable one for a specific MPS. Here, we provide a guide to designing vascularized MPS by comparing current vascularization strategies according to key design drivers, including the microfluidic platform, organotypic vascular architecture, matrix properties, and coculture with perivascular cells. We highlight trade-offs between biological fidelity, engineering control, and translational needs, while considering approaches widely adopted in commercial MPS. Finally, we discuss how close the field is to delivering physiologically accurate vascularized MPS and how emerging omics technologies may redefine vascular identity and functionality.

works.title: Engineering regenerative cell therapy products through biofabrication
works.abstract: Regenerative cell therapies delivered as cell suspensions often face limited survival, retention, and tissue integration. Biofabrication produces structured living products with controlled cellular organization and material environments. Here, we present a product-oriented framework linking fabrication-derived attributes to therapeutic function, delivery compatibility, manufacturing reproducibility, quality control, and safety and regulatory evidence. We distinguish biomaterial-free and biomaterial-based products based on whether exogenous biomaterials are retained as structural or functional components of the administered construct, and examine hybridization as an integration strategy. Comparisons across formats assess whether engineered features provide therapeutic value sufficient to justify added manufacturing and translational burdens. This framework guides product design toward the minimum complexity needed to achieve clinically meaningful function with reproducible manufacture and delivery.

Chloroplast genome engineering: Recent advances, pathways towards commercialization and future directions
works.abstract: Chloroplasts are ideal biofactories because thousands of transgene copies integrated into each plant cell to produce high levels of recombinant proteins and enzymes. Because chloroplast genomes are predominantly maternally inherited, transgenes are generally not transmitted via pollen. Nuclear genome engineering ushered in the GMO revolution for crop protection that mostly required lower levels of transgene expression. Higher level expression and biosafety through gene containment facilitate new applications of GM crops, including production of high-value biopharmaceuticals and enzymes. This review focuses on recent advances in this field, including the first FDA approval of biopharmaceuticals made in plant cells for evaluation in human clinical trials, topical or oral drug delivery, marker free edible plants by removal of antibiotic resistance genes and novel post-translational modifications required to produce functional human proteins. In addition, new tools are discussed to improve DNA delivery, vector free assembly, episomal or integration methods, enhancement of transgene expression through optimization of regulatory sequences, codons, targeted genome editing and other innovations in biomanufacturing. Topical drug delivery using plant cells incorporated into chewing gums to control oral viruses, pathogenic bacteria, or yeast and oral drug delivery with therapeutic proteins made in plant cells to treat diabetes, obesity and cardiopulmonary diseases currently advanced to human clinical trials are discussed. In addition, high-value industrial enzymes for launching new products or to confer valuable agronomic traits or enhance photosynthesis are discussed. Future perspectives section provides examples of biotechnology products anticipated to be launched in the next 3-5 years, with opportunities and anticipated challenges.

Liquid‐Suspendable Metabolic Sensors Allow Real‐Time Oxygen Consumption Monitoring in Caco‐2 and Colon Organoid‐Based Gut‐on‐a‐Chip Models
works.abstract: The organ-on-a-chip field is a rapidly evolving area of expertise, combining enhanced physiological relevance with a wide range of functional readouts across diverse cellular models. One such readout is oxygen metabolism, which serves as a key indicator of mitochondrial function. In this study, we utilized metabolic sensors designed for real-time measurement of oxygen consumption, reflecting aerobic respiration, within a commercially available microfluidic platform. We demonstrated that time-resolved detection of oxygen consumption is feasible within the system's microliter-scale volumes and that chemically induced changes in cellular oxygen metabolism can be monitored in real time in two ready-to-use gut-on-a-chip models. In summary, this novel application of metabolic sensors enables direct evaluation of mitochondrial function in complex cellular environments by addressing key analytical challenges often encountered in organ-on-a-chip systems due to their limited size and structural complexity.

works.title: Redirecting Metabolic Flux to Minimize By‐Product Formation Enables Efficient De Novo Biosynthesis of Chlorogenic Acid in Escherichia coli
works.abstract: Chlorogenic acid (CGA) is an important natural hydroxycinnamic acid ester with diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, antibacterial, and potential antitumor properties. However, efficient microbial titer of CGA remains challenging because of insufficient hydroxylation efficiency, by-product accumulation, and limited host tolerance. Herein, an efficient and sustainable microbial platform for de novo CGA biosynthesis was constructed in Escherichia coli. Enhancement of the NAD(H) biosynthetic pathway increased intracellular reducing power and increased hydroxylation efficiency. A synergistic hydroxylation module consisting of the p-coumarate 3-hydroxylase from Saccharothrix espanaensis (SeC3H) and the flavin reductase from Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PaHpaC)was further introduced to promote the conversion of p-coumaric acid (pCA) to caffeic acid (CA) and redirect metabolic flux toward CGA biosynthesis. Rational engineering of 4-coumarate-CoA ligase from Arabidopsis thaliana (At4CL) increased substrate selectivity and decreased the formation of the major by-product p-coumaroylquinic acid (pCQA). In addition, transcriptomic analysis identified lsrG, a gene associated with the AI-2 quorum-sensing system, as a beneficial target whose overexpression further enhanced CGA titer. The final engineered strain produced 7220.3 mg/L CGA in a 50 L fed-batch fermentation. The strategies developed herein may provide an effective metabolic engineering framework for the sustainable biosynthesis of CGA and other aromatic natural products.

works.title: Systematic Evaluation of Cyanidioschyzon merolae Across Photobioreactor Systems: Linking Reactor Design to Biomass Production and Biochemical Composition
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Extremophilic red microalgae are promising platforms for sustainable biotechnology, combining robust growth under selective thermoacidophilic conditions with production of thermostable phycobiliproteins and carbon‐rich biomass. However, reactor‐dependent effects on growth, product formation, and biomass composition remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we systematically evaluated the extremophilic red microalga Cyanidioschyzon merolae across cultivation scales and reactor formats and benchmarked its performance against the well‐established Galdieria javensis and Limnospira platensis . In small‐scale multi‐cultivator photobioreactors and microfluidic growth chambers, C. merolae showed superior growth, reaching a maximum growth rate of 0.034 ± 0.001 h −1 and 8.3 ± 0.3 g L −1 cell dry weight. Microfluidic cultivation enabled growth analysis at single‐cell resolution and matched growth rates obtained in photobioreactors. To identify scalable production strategies, C. merolae was further cultivated in a flat‐panel photobioreactor (FPR) and a custom‐designed internally illuminated photobioreactor (IIPBR). The custom‐designed photobioreactor delivered the highest biomass concentration and productivity, yielding 11.5 ± 0.6 g L −1 cell dry weight and 1.07 ± 0.06 g L −1 d −1 , and comparable yields with regard to R‐phycocyanin and R‐allophycocyanin (R‐APC). Biomass analysis revealed substantial carbon and nitrogen contents, starch accumulation up to > 20% of cell dry weight, and fatty acids dominated by palmitic, linoleic, and oleic acids. Despite its reduced cell wall fraction, C. merolae contained structurally diverse, cultivation‐dependent polysaccharides. These results establish C. merolae as a versatile chassis for thermostable pigment production and renewable feedstock generation, highlighting photobioreactor design as a key determinant of productivity and biomass quality.

works.title: High Hydrogen Yields During Continuous Photofermentative Valorization of Hydrothermal Carbonization Process Water by Engineered Rhodobacter capsulatus
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Photofermentative hydrogen (H 2 ) production by purple non‐sulphur bacteria (PNSB) is a promising route for sustainable energy generation, although large‐scale application remains limited by substrate costs and process stability. Here, we demonstrate sustained H 2 production using an H 2 ‐overproducing Rhodobacter capsulatus Δ hupAB mutant cultivated on process water (PW) derived from the hydrothermal carbonization of food waste. Batch assays showed that buffered PW supports phototrophic growth, soluble chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal, and H 2 production without requiring defined carbon sources. Based on these results, continuous photofermentation was operated at a hydraulic retention time of 3.5 days using diluted PW supplemented only with phosphate buffer, operating for more than 600 h, with sustained COD removal and H 2 production. Average H 2 yields reached 178 mL H 2 g −1 COD during the stable operational period (100–350 h), comparing favourably with literature values. Carbon partitioning analyses revealed lower inorganic carbon formation under PW feeding, consistent with a redistribution of reducing equivalents towards nitrogenase activity. This behaviour was associated with lower biomass yields and enhanced H 2 production. Minimal CO 2 formation resulted in an almost pure H 2 stream. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous photofermentative valorization of PW for coupling waste valorization with high‐purity biohydrogen production.

works.title: Unravelling the Chemolithoautotrophic Metabolism of the Carboxydotrophic Knallgas Bacterium Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The sustainable production of chemicals is critical to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and environmental pollution. Gaseous feedstocks from industrial waste streams and waste gasification, including CO, CO 2 and H 2 , represent abundant and underutilized resources for biotechnology. Syngas fermentation has been predominantly studied under anaerobic conditions, whereas aerobic processes may offer advantages for the biosynthesis of energy‐intensive products. One promising organism is the aerobic carboxydotroph Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava DSM 1084, whose chemolithoautotrophic metabolism remains poorly understood. To address this, we performed proteome analysis under different growth conditions and characterized deletion mutants of key enzymes involved in CO and H 2 oxidation. Deletion mutants showed that only CO dehydrogenase I and the membrane‐bound hydrogenase are essential for CO and H 2 oxidation, respectively. The role of the putative second CO dehydrogenase remains to be elucidated, and the soluble hydrogenase may contribute to redox balancing under microaerobic or anaerobic conditions. In addition, the H 2 ‐sensing regulatory system appears to be nonfunctional, and the transhydrogenase PntAB supports redox homeostasis during chemolithoautotrophic growth. Electrons from CO or H 2 are transferred via the reduced quinone pool to NADH through proton‐motive force‐driven reverse electron transfer. Nevertheless, growth on CO remains slower than on CO 2 /H 2 . In contrast to CO 2 /H 2 , an unphysiologically high CO concentration (80%) led to a major proteome rearrangement, with 1879 of 3640 reliably quantified proteins showing altered abundance compared to fructose‐grown cells, including a pronounced stress response. Under such conditions, cells are likely to invest additional energy to maintain redox balance. Together with the less energy‐conserving autotrophic branch of the respiratory chain and cytoplasmic CO oxidation, this results in inefficient CO conversion and reduced growth.

works.title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems
works.abstract: ABSTRACT In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage‐encoded anti‐defence against bacterial anti‐phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co‐folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti‐CRISPR‐Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD + . Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD + from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti‐PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti‐Septu). Phages counteract toxin‐antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti‐defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

works.title: Integrated Microbial Profiling Identifies Bacterial and Fungal Communities in Pseudomyxoma Peritonei Mucin
works.abstract: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare mucinous malignancy in which tumour-associated microbial communities remain poorly characterised, particularly, their fungal component and spatial organisation. We applied an integrated workflow combining 16S and 18S rRNA gene sequencing, microbial culture, histochemical staining, chromogenic RNAscope in situ hybridisation and a patient-derived xenograft model to investigate bacterial and fungal communities in control tissues and low- and high-grade PMP mucin. Bacterial and fungal DNA was detected in PMP-associated mucin, with grade-associated differences in bacterial composition and predicted functional potential. Viable bacteria were recovered from human PMP samples and xenograft-derived mucin. Fungal structures were independently supported by periodic acid-Schiff and Calcofluor White staining, while RNAscope localised bacterial 16S and fungal 18S rRNA signals within epithelial and mucin-rich tumour regions. Comparable microbial signals were observed in the xenograft model. Together, these complementary approaches identify PMP mucin as a multi-kingdom microbial niche and provide the first characterisation of its associated mycobiome. This integrated analytical framework may facilitate the investigation of microorganisms in other low-biomass, mucin-rich tumour environments and provides a basis for future mechanistic studies of microbe-host interactions in PMP.

works.title: Genetic Engineering Efforts to Generate Chlamydomonas Strains for Large‐Scale Biomolecule Production
works.abstract: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is an established model microalga. Its easy manipulation, metabolic flexibility and tractable genomes allowed researchers to investigate fundamental processes such as photosynthesis using genetic studies for decades. Chlamydomonas is not naturally rich in lipids or pigments compared to industrially relevant microalgae. However, we highlight how its biotechnological potential relies on advanced genetic and metabolic engineering strategies, now possible due to the availability of extensive toolbox and synthetic biology platforms, which can improve industrial traits and allow to produce a variety of biomolecules of biotechnological interest. We provide examples of biomolecule production (terpenoids and recombinant proteins), and show that productivities (mg/L) are in the same range or could even be higher than those reached in other photosynthetic chassis (e.g., cyanobacteria or mosses). We point out that despite these achievements, the industrial implementation of C. reinhardtii is still lacking. Further technological advancements as well as clear international regulations and social acceptance are fundamental to reach the full potential of this microalga.

works.title: Reprogramming Native Cryptic Plasmids Enables Antibiotic‐Selection‐Free Urate Degradation by Escherichia coli Nissle 1917
works.abstract: Hyperuricemia is associated with renal injury and disturbances in gut microbial ecology. Intestinal urate clearance by engineered probiotics is limited by antibiotic-free functional maintenance and the oxygen requirement of urate oxidase (UOX). We reprogrammed the native cryptic plasmids of Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) to construct M12U, a marker-free dual-plasmid strain. pMUT2 carried an HucR-regulated urate-responsive UOX module, while pMUT1 encoded a low-oxygen-responsive UOX module and Tat-targeted Vitreoscilla haemoglobin (tat-VHB). M12U degraded urate in vitro and retained activity under low-oxygen conditions. In hyperuricemic mice (n = 5 per group), oral M12U reduced serum urate, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, inflammatory cytokines and renal histopathological injury. 16S rRNA profiling showed increased microbial richness and a partial shift in community composition toward healthy controls. Shotgun metagenomics revealed enrichment of Lactobacillus johnsonii and Bacteroides acidifaciens, together with increased metabolic potential related to the pentose phosphate pathway and glutathione metabolism. Faecal metabolomics showed reduced uric acid abundance and increased thiamine monophosphate and argininosuccinic acid. These results support further evaluation of dual-native-plasmid architectures for gut-directed urate clearance.

works.title: Correction to ‘Eco‐Microbiology: A Frugal‐Circular Framework for Biosafe, Low‐Cost Practical Microbiology in Secondary Education’
Biofilm Engineering for Efficient Substrate‐Enzyme Interactions to Enhance Enzymatic PET Degradation
works.abstract: Despite extensive protein engineering efforts to significantly increase the catalytic efficiency of plastic-degrading enzymes, inefficient plastic-enzyme interactions during the interfacial biocatalytic process continue to impede their widespread applications. Here, we engineered the complete csgBACEFG curli operon through multicopy chromosomal integration to generate a csgBACEFG-optimized (CSGO) biofilm with enhanced curli assembly and plastic-surface adhesion. Unlike previou curli-based enzyme immobilization studies using individual CsgA curli components or pre-existing curli scaffolds, our strategy uses the complete curli assembly machinery to construct a dense, surface-associated catalytic biofilm. FAST-PETase was then embedded in a 2-day PET-surface CSGO biofilm through the SpyTag/SpyCatcher system, producing 2.5-fold more hydrolysis products from PET film depolymerization than soluble FAST-PETase with the same initial enzyme mass. The carrier-free biofilm-supported FAST-PETase also retained more than 50% of its first-cycle product formation after five 24-h PET nanoplastic (NanoPET) degradation cycles. These findings support biofilm-mediated enhancement of PET depolymerization and provide a proof-of-concept strategy that may inform future biofilm-assisted plastic treatment.

works.title: Riboflavin Metabolism Links Metabolic State to Biofilm Development, Cell‐Envelope Homeostasis, and Antimicrobial Susceptibility in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Biofilm formation and phenotypic drug tolerance contribute to the persistence and treatment challenges associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( M. tb ). Although M. tb lacks canonical quorum‐sensing systems, it exhibits coordinated metabolic and cell‐envelope adaptations during biofilm development, suggesting the existence of alternative mechanisms linking cellular metabolism to multicellular behaviour. Here, using a combination of functional genomics, metabolic perturbation and systems‐level analyses, we identify riboflavin metabolism as a regulatory axis influencing biofilm development and antimicrobial susceptibility in M. tb . CRISPRi‐mediated knockdown and targeted overexpression of riboflavin biosynthetic genes markedly altered biofilm architecture, cell morphology, envelope ultrastructure, membrane permeability and lipid composition, with ribA2 and ribF emerging as potential metabolic vulnerabilities. Exogenous riboflavin enhanced biofilm formation, whereas the riboflavin antimetabolite roseoflavin suppressed this phenotype. Notably, cell‐free supernatants from late‐stage cultures, accumulated higher levels of riboflavin and restored biofilm formation in a riboflavin‐biosynthesis‐deficient strain, supporting a diffusible regulatory function beyond the established metabolic roles of riboflavin‐derived FMN and FAD. Integrated transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses revealed coordinated reprogramming of biofilm‐associated regulatory pathways, cell‐envelope lipid metabolism and the F 420 biosynthetic network, accompanied by increased susceptibility to anti‐tuberculosis drugs. Molecular docking further identified potential interactions of riboflavin with regulatory proteins associated with biofilm and stress‐response pathways. Together, these findings establish riboflavin metabolism as a previously underappreciated regulatory layer connecting microbial metabolism, biofilm development, cell‐envelope homeostasis and drug tolerance. This metabolic axis provides a potential framework for developing microbial biotechnology‐based strategies to interfere with biofilm‐associated persistence and improve the efficacy of anti‐tuberculosis therapeutics.

works.title: Succession of Microbial Communities and Identification of Indigenous PAH‐Tolerant Bacteria Under Multiple PAH Stresses in Mangrove Sediments From Maowei Sea, Guangxi, China
works.abstract: Elucidating microbial community shifts under polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) stress and screening indigenous PAH-tolerant microbial resources are valuable for exploring potential bioremediation strategies for PAH-contaminated mangrove ecosystems. In this study, surface sediments were collected from mangrove wetlands of the Maowei Sea, Guangxi, China. Three rounds of successive 7-day enrichment cultures were performed with gradually elevated PAH concentrations using phenanthrene, anthracene, and pyrene as target carbon substrates, followed by isolation and taxonomic identification of PAH-adapted bacteria. The results demonstrated that microbial community diversity decreased with increasing enrichment rounds and varied significantly among different PAH substrate treatments. ANOSIM confirmed significant differences in community structure across enrichment cycles and PAH treatments (p < 0.01), consistent with the ordination patterns revealed by Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS). The PAH-adapted microbial communities were predominantly dominated by Pseudomonadota (33.2%-99.9%), Bacillota (0%-48.3%), and Actinomycetota (0.1%-33.7%). In total, 17 indigenous PAH-tolerant bacterial strains belonging to eight genera within the phylum Pseudomonadota were isolated, with representative strains affiliated with Labrys, Sphingomonas, and Acinetobacter. Within the tested physiological gradient ranges, Labrys sp. F3-1 and Acinetobacter sp. B1-5 exhibited optimal growth at pH 5.0, 40°C, and 15‰ salinity, while Sphingomonas sp. N2-15 showed the best growth performance at pH 5.0, 25°C, and 4‰ salinity. Growth assays under PAH pressure further verified that these three isolates could survive and proliferate in PAH-amended selective media under the tested laboratory conditions. This study provides indigenous PAH-tolerant bacterial resources and fundamental community-level insights for future investigations on microbial-based remediation of PAH-polluted mangrove sediments. Notably, the high PAH concentrations applied during laboratory enrichment (100-500 mg/L) were substantially higher than in situ environmental levels; the observed microbial responses and strain physiological traits reflect adaptive characteristics under extreme laboratory selective pressure and should be cautiously extrapolated to natural mangrove ecosystems.
